You can modify the training process further by using different arguments. Setting loss_balance_class_weights to TRUE adjusts the weights of the classes/categories according to the ‘Inverse Class Frequency’ method. This option should be activated if you are dealing with imbalanced data.

Enabling the loss_balance_sequence_length option can improve performance when dealing with texts of different lengths with imbalanced frequencies. When this option is enabled, the loss is adjusted according to the ‘Inverse Class Frequency’ method, based on the absolute frequencies of the lengths of your texts.

The parameter epochs determines the maximum number of epochs. During training, the model with the most balanced accuracy is saved and used.

The value of the parameter batch_size determines the number of cases to be processed simultaneously. It is a very important parameter that significantly impacts the model’s performance due to the generalisation gap (Keskar et al. 2017, p. 2). This describes the observation that models trained with a large batch size tend to perform poorly on test data sets compared to those trained with a small batch size (Keskar et al. 2017, p. 3). A study by Masters and Luschi (2018) suggests how to determine an optimal batch size when using SGD as an optimizer. Their study shows that smaller batch sizes offer more stable and reliable training, while also achieving better generalisation performance. Batch sizes between 4 and 32 lead to the best performance. In practice, however, we need large batch sizes to efficiently use computer hardware and save time and energy. Therefore, the aim is to use the largest possible batch size while achieving good generalisation performance. To achieve this, use large batch sizes and large dropout values. Please note that there are exceptions to this rule. In the context of contrastive learning, for example, higher batch sizes tend to generate better generalisation performance (Chen et al. 2020).For more details please refer to the vignette 04 Model configuration and training

We set lr_rate and lr_min to 0.0 to request an automatic calculation of a suitable learning rate.

To speed up computations, we activate Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) with gradient scaling by setting amp = TRUE. In general, we recommend activating mixed precision. If you encounter any problems, turn this option off.

Since training a neural net is energy-consuming, aifeducation allows you to estimate its ecological impact with the help of the Python library ‘codecarbon.’ Thus, the sustain_track parameter is set to TRUE by default. If you use the sustainability tracker, you must provide the three-letter code for the country in which your computer is located (e.g. “CAN” for Canada, “DEU” for Germany). You can find a list of these codes on Wikipedia. This is because different countries use different sources and techniques for generating energy, resulting in a specific impact on CO₂ emissions. For the USA and Canada, you can also specify a region by setting sustain_region. Please refer to the ‘codecarbon’ documentation for more information.

Finally, the trace and ml_trace options allow you to control how much information about the training process is printed to the console.

Please note that training the classifier can take some time. If options such as generating synthetic cases (use_sc) or pseudo-labelling (use_pl) are disabled, the training process is shorter.

After performance estimation, the final training of the classifier uses all available data. In other words, the test sample is left empty.

To visualise the progress of the training, you can request a plot showing how important performance measures develop over epochs. You can choose from the following measures: classifier’s loss ("loss"), accuracy ("accuracy"), balanced accuracy ("balanced_accuracy"), and average iota ("avg_iota"). Set final_training=FALSE to request the mean values of all the folds used during the performance estimation phase.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 11: Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (loss)

Figure 11 shows the development of the loss averaged across all folds. In general, the training curve should decrease to zero. The curves for the validation and test samples should also decrease, but then start to increase after a certain point. The rectangles indicate the state of the model selected as the best during a fold.

Since there are some measures that provide a better post-hoc analysis than the loss, you can request further plots. The following plot shows the development of the average iota for all categories/classes.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 12: Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (iota)

The average iota ranges between 0 and 1 and indicates how well the predictions represent the true values. Higher values indicate better performance. Since measures such as average iota are based on discrete values that can fluctuate significantly, you can plot a smoothed version of average iota, which is more precise.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "s_avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 13: Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (smoothed iota)

To view the final training stage, set final_training to TRUE, as shown in the following figures.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 14: Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (loss)

The dotted line indicates the final model state. Please note that this state is not always the one with the lowest validation loss value, because the best model is selected by applying several criteria in a hierarchical order. The first criterion is the model’s performance in terms of the smoothed average iota The second criterion is the loss.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 15: Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (iota) 

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "s_avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

Figure 16: Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (smoothed iota)

To gain a deeper insight into the training process, you can request a plot visualising the learning rate calculation. Please note that this plot is only available if you have set either lr_rate or lr_min to 0.0.

classifier$plot_learning_rate()

Figure 17: Analysis of Different Learning Rates

The bars in the plot show the percentage increase or decrease in loss compared to the initial loss. The values express the percentage change from the initial loss. A decrease is desirable. The points on the plot show a smoothed distribution of the loss. All calculations for selecting good maximum and minimum learning rates are based on the smoothed data. The automatic calculation selects the learning rate from the range of learning rates that leads to the greatest decrease in loss. The maximum learning rate is set at the point where the decrease in loss turns. The minimum learning rate is set to the rate that results in the smallest reduction in loss. Depending on the learning rate scheduler, other points may be chosen.

7.3 Performance Evaluation

Once training is complete, you can evaluate the performance of the classifier. For each fold, the classifier is applied to the test sample and the results are compared to the true categories/classes. As the test sample is never part of the training set, all performance measures provide a more realistic idea of the classifier’s performance.

To help researchers judge the quality of the predictions, aifeducation uses several measures and concepts from content analysis. These are:

  • Iota Concept of the Second Generation (Berding & Pargmann 2022).
  • Krippendorff’s Alpha (Krippendorff 2019).
  • Percentage Agreement.
  • Gwet’s AC1/AC2 (Gwet 2014).
  • Kendall’s coefficient of concordance W.
  • Cohen’s Kappa unweighted (Cohen 1960).
  • Cohen’s Kappa with equal weights (Cohen 1968).
  • Cohen’s Kappa with squared weights (Cohen 1968).
  • Fleiss’ Kappa for multiple raters without exact estimation (Fleiss 1971).

You can access the mean values across all folds via reliability$test_metric_mean. In our example, this would be:

classifier$reliability$test_metric_mean
#>           iota_index            min_iota2            avg_iota2 
#>            0.5636364            0.4584307            0.5906369 
#>            max_iota2            min_alpha            avg_alpha 
#>            0.7228431            0.5589286            0.7194643 
#>            max_alpha    static_iota_index   dynamic_iota_index 
#>            0.8800000            0.2818290            0.4751055 
#>       kalpha_nominal       kalpha_ordinal              kendall 
#>            0.4688048            0.4688048            0.7365683 
#>   c_kappa_unweighted       c_kappa_linear      c_kappa_squared 
#>            0.4622487            0.4622487            0.4622487 
#>         kappa_fleiss percentage_agreement    balanced_accuracy 
#>            0.4567024            0.7729249            0.7194643 
#>     gwet_ac1_nominal      gwet_ac2_linear   gwet_ac2_quadratic 
#>            0.6083801            0.6083801            0.6083801 
#>        avg_precision           avg_recall               avg_f1 
#>            0.7594686            0.7194643            0.7283512

An addition, standard measures from machine learning are reported. These are

  • Precision
  • Recall
  • F1-Score

You can access these values as follows:

classifier$reliability$standard_measures_mean
#>     precision    recall        f1
#> neg 0.7172222 0.5589286 0.6195679
#> pos 0.8017151 0.8800000 0.8371345

To analyse the quality of the training across all folds, you can request an additional box plot. The figure below shows the performance that the classifier achieved.

classifier$plot_reliability_distribution(measures="all")

Figure 18: Box Plot of Performance Measures

Finally, you can plot a coding stream scheme to show how cases in different classes are labelled.

classifier$plot_coding_stream()

Figure 19: Coding Stream of the Classifier

Evaluating the performance of a classifier is a complex task that goes beyond the scope of this vignette. If you would like to delve deeper into this topic, we recommend consulting the cited literature on content analysis and machine learning.

7.4 Sustainability

If the classifier was trained with an active sustainability tracker, you can retrieve sustainability information by calling classifier$get_sustainability_data().

# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(classifier$get_sustainability_data())

7.5 Saving and Loading a Classifier

The saving and loading process follows the same pattern as for the other objects. aifeducation. You can save the classifier by calling the save_to_disk function. In our example, this might look like this:

save_to_disk(
  object = classifier,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "cls_imdb_movie_reviews"
)

The classifier is saved to examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews. To load the model call load_from_disk.

classifier <- load_from_disk("examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews")

7.6 Predicting New Data

If you would like to apply your classifier to new data, two steps are necessary. First, you must transform the raw text into a numerical representation using exactly the same text embedding model that was used to train your classifier (see Section 4). In the case of our example classifier, we use our BERT model.

# If our model is not loaded
tem <- load_from_disk("examples/eurobert_te_model")

# Create a numerical representation of the text
review_embeddings <- tem$embed_large(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  trace = TRUE
)
#> Calculating Embeddings  10.00 % (1|10) done ETA: 0000::00::17Calculating Embeddings  20.00 % (2|10) done ETA: 0000::00::12Calculating Embeddings  30.00 % (3|10) done ETA: 0000::00::10Calculating Embeddings  40.00 % (4|10) done ETA: 0000::00::08Calculating Embeddings  50.00 % (5|10) done ETA: 0000::00::07Calculating Embeddings  60.00 % (6|10) done ETA: 0000::00::05Calculating Embeddings  70.00 % (7|10) done ETA: 0000::00::04Calculating Embeddings  80.00 % (8|10) done ETA: 0000::00::03Calculating Embeddings  90.00 % (9|10) done ETA: 0000::00::01Calculating Embeddings  100.00 % (10|10) done ETA: 0000::00::00

To transform raw text into a numeric representation, simply pass the text to the embed_large method of the loaded model. The raw text should be an object of the class LargeDataSetForText. To create such a data set, please refer to Section 2.

The resulting object can then be passed to the predict method of our classifier to obtain predictions together with an estimate of certainty for each class/category.

# If your classifier is not loaded
classifier <- load_from_disk("examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews")

# predict the classes of new texts
predicted_categories <- classifier$predict(
  newdata = review_embeddings,
  batch_size = 32
)

# Show predicted categories
head(predicted_categories)
#>             neg         pos expected_category
#> 11329 0.9984832 0.001516801               neg
#> 10460 0.9984681 0.001531932               neg
#> 10536 0.9989967 0.001003357               neg
#> 12035 0.9976599 0.002340015               neg
#> 7267  0.9985479 0.001452108               neg
#> 4761  0.9977448 0.002255289               neg

# Count frequencies
table(predicted_categories$expected_category)
#> 
#> neg pos 
#>  97 203

Once the prediction has been made by the classifier, the estimated categories/classes are stored as ‘predicted_categories’. This object is a data.frame containing text IDs in the rows and the probabilities of the different categories/classes in the columns. The final column, named ‘expected_category’, represents the category assigned to a text with the highest probability.

These estimates can be used in further analyses employing common methods from the educational and social sciences, such as correlation analysis, regression analysis, structural equation modelling, latent class analysis, and analysis of variance.

Now you are ready to to use aifeducation.

8 Plots for Training History

8.1 BaseModels

You can use BaseModels, TEFeatureExtractors and classifiers to create plots showing your model’s training process. The process of requesting these plots is similar for all objects. However, classifiers offer the greatest degree of customisation of graphics. This chapter demonstrates how to use the plots. We refer to models from previous chapters to provide examples.

We start with the base models. The x_min, x_max, y_min and y_max arguments allow you to zoom in or out. If you set these arguments to NULL, the values will be determined automatically.

The ind_best_model argument allows you to emphasise the epoch with the lowest loss for the validation sample. In general, this is the state of the model with the best generalisation abilities. Unlike the classifiers, this is also the final state of the model after training. The text_size argument allows you to increase or decrease the size of the text within the graphic.

base_model_bert$plot_training_history(
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 20: Example of a Training History for a BaseModel emphasizing the Best Model State.

8.2 Classifiers

Classifiers offer a greater variety of options. Using the x_min, x_max, y_min and y_max arguments, you can specify the area to be plotted. Setting these arguments to NULL will generate adequate values automatically. With the measure argument, you can select the metric you would like to see. For example, the following plot shows loss.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 21: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss.

The following plot shows how the average iota values changed over the course of the training process.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 22: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota.

Setting ind_best_model to TRUE will display additional points in the graphic. These points represents the epochs and their corresponding values according to the chosen metric at which the model performed best. For metrics such as loss, the values should be close to 0, while for metrics such as accuracy, balanced accuracy and average iota, the best values are close to 1. You can see one point for every fold during training.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 23: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss and the best Model States. 

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 24: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota and the best Model States.

Please note that these points indicate the model’s optimal state according to the chosen metric for each fold. However, these values do not necessarily reflect the final state of the model. This is because the best state of a model during each training loop is determined by the best smoothed average iota value. If there are multiple models with the same smoothed average iota value, the model with the best loss is taken into account. Finally, the state with the highest number of epochs is used.

Set ind_selected_model to TRUE to add the final states of the model for every fold.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 25: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss, the best Model States, and the Final Model States.

Since the performance of a model is determined by several factors, the minimum and maximum values provide a deeper understanding of the training process. To include these in the plot, set add_min_max to TRUE. The plot will now show the full range of values for each epoch according to the chosen metric.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 26: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss with Minimal and Maximal Values.

Using the argument final_training, you can switch between the performance estimation stage and the final training stage of the model. Since the final training phase only differentiates between training and validation data sets, there is no line for test data. In addition, there are no folds. Therefore, the argument add_min_max has no functionality.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 27: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss at the Final Training Phase.

The final important argument is pl_step. This value is only relevant if the model used pseudo labeling during training. This parameter allows you to select the step during pseudo labeling that should be displayed in the plot. This works for performance estimation as well as the final training stage.
